The study investigates the effect of solidification direction on ice-templated microstructures.
The researchers found that upward solidification leads to microstructural inhomogeneities.
Downward and horizontal solidification do not lead to microstructural inhomogeneities.
The density gradient in water creates a non-monotonic temperature profile during directional solidification.
The particle size and concentration in the suspension affect the microstructure of the material.
The freezing substrate temperature does not significantly affect the solidification process.
The average solidification velocity is 75±10 μm⋅s-1.
The macroscopic porosity decreases with increasing weight fractions of TiO.
The study provides insights into the ice-templating technique and its applications in materials science.
The researchers used a mixture of ethylene glycol and ammonium hydroxide as dispersants and agar as a binder.
The suspensions were solidified under three conditions: upward, downward, and horizontal to the gravity vector.
The solidification times were estimated by visual inspection at ~35-45 s.
The samples were sintered in a box furnace at 1173 K for 1 h in air.
The researchers used scanning electron and optical microscopy to examine the microstructure of the samples.
The study found that the microstructure of the samples was affected by the solidification direction and the particle size and concentration in the suspension.
